newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik talks delayed after opposition chief held up.
newsitem.headline: Tajik talks delayed after opposition chief held up.

text.p: Peace negotiations between Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri scheduled for Monday have been postponed because Nuri is stuck in the Afghan town of Kandahar, a Tajik official said.
Nuri was travelling in a United Nations aircraft on Saturday to the talks in northern Afghanistan when jets of Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban militia forced it to land.
The Taleban said on Sunday the plane had been released and authorised to fly on.
"Due to Nuri's delay with the Taleban, the meeting has been postponed," Rakhmonov's spokesman, Zafar Saidov, told Reuters in the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
The talks' delay was also confirmed by a spokesman for the Tajik Islamist opposition based in Dushanbe, Abdunabi Sattorzoda. "He (Nuri) is a guest of the Taleban," he said.
Both Saidov and Sattorzoda said the two leaders would try to meet in the northern Afghan town of Kunduz on Tuesday.

Sattorzoda, a member of a United Nations commission in Dushanbe which monitors a much flouted ceasefire, said fighting between Tajik government forces and Islamist guerrillas continued to rage around the town of Garm on Monday, around 200 km (130 miles) east of the Tajik capital.
But Milos Strugar, Senior Political Officer with the U.N. military observer mission in Tajikistan (UNMOT), stressed the talks had not been called off.
"The meeting between Nuri and Rakhmonov has not been cancelled," Strugar told Reuters. "We are working on it."
He said a United Nations aircraft would attempt to fly Nuri to Kunduz later on Monday.
There is little trust between the two sides and diplomats based in Dushanbe have been pessimistic about the outcome of the talks.
Fighting has flared in the former Soviet republic since the talks were announced at the end of last month as each side moves to strengthen its hand at the negotiating table.

There have also been a spate of attacks against Russian servicemen based in the former Soviet republic, who help prop up Rakhmonov's shaky administration. The opposition is widely held to have been responsible.

Tens of thousands have been killed and many more made homeless in the bitter four-year civil war in the mountainous country bordering Afghanistan and China. Regional and clan rivalries underlie the conflict between the Islamist rebels and the secular government.
